Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) -- The sponsor of a proposal to rein in aggressive celebrity photographers is meeting resistance from Los Angeles' top cop, who says the law is not needed when celebrities just behave. Photographers swarm a car carrying Britney Spears after a Los Angeles court appearance in October 2007. City Councilman Dennis Zine wants to require photographers to stay a safe distance from celebrities. His proposed ordinance is nicknamed the "Britney Law" for the hordes of paparazzi that swarm around pop star Britney Spears, sometimes costing the city thousands of dollars for escorts and other enforcement. "They act like a pack of wolves stalking their prey, creating havoc in the streets, and are nuisances to innocent bystanders," Zine said at a task force hearing he convened Thursday.  Watch how paparazzi spy on Hollywood stars » . The proposal gained exposure last month when officials from around Southern California asked former independent counsel Kenneth Starr -- whose investigation of former President Clinton spawned its own share of tabloid headlines -- to help craft a law that would protect celebrities without infringing on freedom of the press.  iReport.com: Share your celeb stories and photos . Critics of the plan include Los Angeles Police Chief William Bratton, who argues that it would be difficult to enforce. He also says existing laws can keep unruly packs of photographers in check. The chief said the city's tabloid darlings could help by providing photographers less to work with. "If celebrities behave themselves, that solves about 90 percent of the problem," Bratton said. "Britney, the last couple of days, has started wearing clothes again. The paparazzi are leaving town because she's not as interesting when she's not running around without her underwear on." He said actress Lindsay Lohan "evidently found a new love life, so she's probably in New York hanging out" and that "God knows" where billionaire heiress Paris Hilton had been. "She's thankfully disappeared from the scene," Bratton said. At the hearing, members of the paparazzi also said the law would be impossible to enforce. "Unless every celebrity has a chaperone of a police officer with a 6-foot tape measure, how are you going to enforce it?" said photographer Nick Stern. Those attending included musician John Mayer, actor Eric Roberts, sheriff's officials, representatives of the Screen Actors Guild and officials from West Hollywood, Beverly Hills and Malibu. CNN's Kareen Wynter contributed to this report.

The issue has drawn attention amid scenes such as the October 2007 mob of photographers surrounding a vehicle carrying Britney Spears after a court appearance in Los Angeles.

Councilman Dennis Zine is proposing an ordinance that would force photographers to maintain a safe space between themselves and celebrities. The measure has been dubbed the “Britney Law” because of the large groups of paparazzi that frequently pursue Spears. Managing those crowds has sometimes required police escorts and other enforcement measures costing the city thousands of dollars.

During a task force hearing he organized Thursday, Zine compared the photographers to wolves hunting prey, saying they disrupt traffic and public spaces while troubling uninvolved people nearby. CNN also offered video showing the methods paparazzi use to monitor Hollywood celebrities.

The idea received broader publicity the previous month after officials across Southern California approached Kenneth Starr for help writing legislation that would safeguard famous people without violating press freedoms. “If celebrities behave themselves, that solves about 90 percent of the problem,” he said. Bratton added that Spears had begun wearing clothes again in recent days and claimed paparazzi were leaving because she was less compelling when she was no longer appearing in public without underwear.

The chief also remarked that actress Lindsay Lohan had apparently entered a new romantic relationship and was likely spending time in New York. As for billionaire heiress Paris Hilton, he said only “God knows” where she had been and expressed relief that she had vanished from public view.

Paparazzi who spoke at the hearing likewise argued that the proposed restriction could not realistically be policed. Photographer Nick Stern questioned how authorities could apply it unless every celebrity were accompanied by an officer carrying a six-foot measuring tape.

Others present included musician John Mayer, actor Eric Roberts, sheriff’s department personnel, Screen Actors Guild representatives, and officials from Malibu, Beverly Hills and West Hollywood.

CNN’s Kareen Wynter contributed to the report.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about Los Angeles City Councilman Dennis Zine’s proposed “Britney Law” to restrict aggressive paparazzi, including objections from LAPD Chief William Bratton.
counterfactuals.output:
**Los Angeles councilman proposes ‘Britney Law’ to rein in paparazzi**

**LOS ANGELES (CNN)** — A Los Angeles city councilman is proposing new restrictions on aggressive celebrity photographers, citing the media frenzy surrounding pop star Britney Spears as evidence that existing rules do not adequately protect public safety.

Councilman Dennis Zine’s proposal — dubbed the “Britney Law” — would explore creating a legally enforceable safety zone between paparazzi and the celebrities they pursue. Zine said swarms of photographers can block streets, surround vehicles and endanger stars, bystanders and other motorists.

The measure would also target conduct such as reckless driving, trespassing and obstructing sidewalks in the effort to obtain celebrity photographs.

“This is not about stopping people from taking pictures,” Zine said in promoting the plan. “It’s about safety and preventing situations from getting out of control.”

Los Angeles Police Chief William Bratton, however, objected to the proposal, arguing that police already have sufficient laws to deal with dangerous or illegal behavior. Reckless driving, assault, trespassing and obstruction can all be prosecuted under existing statutes, he said.

Bratton also raised concerns about the practicality of enforcing a special buffer zone and warned against adopting rules that could infringe on freedom of the press. He suggested that intense paparazzi attention often diminishes when celebrities avoid highly public behavior.

Representatives of news and photography organizations have similarly argued that broad restrictions could interfere with legitimate newsgathering. Paparazzi critics counter that increasingly aggressive tactics have turned celebrity coverage into a public-safety problem rather than simply a privacy dispute.

The proposal would require further review and approval by the City Council before any restrictions could take effect.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the controversy surrounding a proposed Los Angeles ordinance requiring celebrity photographers to maintain a safe distance from stars, using quotes from officials and paparazzi.
counterfactuals.output:
The proposal sought to create a mandatory “personal safety zone” between celebrities and photographers, responding to complaints that paparazzi swarm stars, block sidewalks and provoke dangerous car chases. Los Angeles Councilman Dennis Zine framed it as a safety measure rather than a ban on photography: “This is about public safety,” he said, arguing that aggressive conduct—not picture-taking itself—was the target.

Critics said existing laws against stalking, assault, reckless driving and obstruction were sufficient. Then–LAPD Chief William Bratton said, “We don’t need any new laws,” contending that enforcement and celebrities’ own publicity-seeking behavior were bigger issues.

Paparazzi likewise described the plan as “ridiculous” and “unenforceable.” They argued that a fixed-distance rule would be difficult to apply on crowded streets or at red-carpet events, could criminalize ordinary news gathering, and singled out celebrity photographers in ways that threatened First Amendment rights. Supporters countered that press freedom does not justify intimidation or conduct that endangers celebrities, photographers and bystanders.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an article about the 2008 task force hearing on paparazzi behavior attended by John Mayer, Eric Roberts, law-enforcement representatives, and Southern California officials.
counterfactuals.output:
# John Mayer, Eric Roberts Join 2008 Los Angeles Hearing on Paparazzi Conduct

In 2008, as confrontations between celebrities and photographers became a near-daily feature of entertainment news, Southern California officials convened a public hearing to examine whether aggressive paparazzi behavior required new laws—or simply stronger enforcement of existing ones.

The hearing brought together musicians and actors, law-enforcement representatives, municipal officials and residents from communities where celebrity photography had become a persistent public-safety concern. Among the best-known participants were singer-songwriter John Mayer and actor Eric Roberts.

At the center of the discussion were familiar complaints: photographers driving recklessly while pursuing celebrities, blocking streets and sidewalks, crowding entrances to restaurants and schools, and provoking subjects in hopes of capturing more valuable images. Officials from Los Angeles and neighboring jurisdictions also confronted a practical problem: paparazzi activity routinely crossed city boundaries, making a single local ordinance difficult to enforce consistently.

Mayer offered one of the hearing’s more measured perspectives. Although he acknowledged the disruption caused by being followed, he cautioned against treating celebrity photography itself as unlawful. Public figures, he argued, could not reasonably expect complete freedom from attention in public places. The more workable response was to establish clear standards of conduct and enforce traffic, trespassing and harassment laws when photographers crossed the line.

His appearance drew unusual attention because Mayer was then a frequent target of celebrity photographers. Rather than demanding a broad ban, he emphasized rules that could distinguish legitimate newsgathering from dangerous conduct.

Roberts presented a more personal account of paparazzi intrusiveness. He described the effect that aggressive photographers could have not only on performers but also on their relatives and neighborhoods. His testimony underscored a recurring theme of the hearing: even when celebrities accepted public scrutiny as part of their profession, family members and bystanders had not necessarily made the same bargain.

Law-enforcement representatives generally stressed that many of the most troubling actions were already prohibited. Speeding, reckless driving, obstructing traffic, trespassing, assault and credible threats could be addressed under existing statutes. The challenge, they said, was gathering evidence, identifying individual offenders and deploying officers quickly enough to stop behavior that often unfolded in moving vehicles.

Southern California officials nevertheless considered whether additional measures were needed. Proposals discussed during the broader 2008 debate included buffer zones around celebrities, licensing or identification requirements for commercial photographers, stronger penalties for reckless pursuit, and coordinated enforcement among Los Angeles, Beverly Hills, West Hollywood, Malibu and other paparazzi hot spots.

The hearing also exposed the legal difficulty of regulating the profession. Paparazzi photographers argued that overly broad restrictions could violate constitutional protections for photography and press activity in public spaces. News organizations warned that rules aimed at celebrity photographers might also affect journalists covering crimes, disasters, demonstrations and government officials.

No single proposal emerged as an immediate solution. Instead, the hearing illustrated the competing interests surrounding celebrity culture in Los Angeles: public safety, privacy, press freedom and the commercial demand for candid photographs.

The 2008 proceedings helped shift the conversation away from annoyance alone and toward conduct that created measurable risks. In the years that followed, California adopted tougher protections in specific areas, including laws addressing dangerous driving for commercial images and stronger safeguards against photographing the children of public figures in harassing ways.

The presence of Mayer and Roberts ensured substantial media coverage, but the hearing’s larger significance lay in its recognition that the paparazzi problem extended beyond celebrities. At issue were public roads, residential neighborhoods, police resources and the safety of anyone caught in the path of a profitable photograph.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: What was the proposed “Britney Law,” why did Dennis Zine support it, and why did Police Chief William Bratton and photographer Nick Stern argue that it would be unnecessary or difficult to enforce?
counterfactuals.output:
The proposed **“Britney Law”** was Los Angeles Councilman Dennis Zine’s 2008 proposal to curb aggressive paparazzi behavior after photographers repeatedly mobbed Britney Spears. It contemplated a legally enforceable **personal-safety or buffer zone—often described as about 20 feet—around celebrities**, with penalties for photographers who crowded, chased, or obstructed them.

Zine, a former police officer, said the issue was **public safety, not celebrity privacy**. Paparazzi scrums involved reckless driving, blocked streets and sidewalks, endangered bystanders, and forced the city to devote police officers and other resources to routine celebrity movements and emergencies.

Police Chief **William Bratton** argued that a new law was unnecessary because police could already use laws against reckless driving, trespassing, assault, obstruction, and similar conduct. He also suggested that celebrities and their handlers sometimes helped create the spectacles.

Photographer **Nick Stern** argued that a fixed buffer would be impractical: in crowded public places it would be hard to determine who was a paparazzo, who counted as a celebrity, and who had crossed the prescribed distance. A celebrity could also walk toward a photographer, effectively putting the photographer in violation. Thus, he viewed the measure as both difficult to enforce and potentially restrictive of legitimate newsgathering.
